description: Lists are the universal data structure of the Wolfram Language: vectors, matrices, tensors, sequences and records are all nested lists. This category covers building lists, measuring and indexing them, restructuring them, and the searching, sorting and grouping operations that make up most list-oriented code.

tools.name: List
tools.description: The fundamental container of the Wolfram Language, written with curly braces as {e1, e2, ...}. Lists are heterogeneous and arbitrarily nested, and are used to represent vectors, matrices, tensors, tuples and sequences of results. Because List is Protected but not Orderless, element order is always preserved, and most built-in numeric functions are Listable so they thread over lists automatically.
tools.notes: {...} is just input syntax for List[...]; FullForm[{1,2}] shows List[1,2]. Nested lists of uniform numeric type are automatically stored as packed arrays for speed.

tools.name: Range
tools.description: Generates a list of evenly spaced values. Range[n] gives {1, 2, ..., n}; Range[a, b] counts from a to b in steps of 1; Range[a, b, da] uses an explicit step, which may be negative, rational or symbolic. It is the standard way to create index lists and sample grids, and works with exact numbers, machine reals and Quantity objects.
tools.usage:
Range[imax]
Range[imin, imax]
Range[imin, imax, di]

parameters.name: imax
parameters.description: Upper bound; the last element is the largest value not exceeding it.

parameters.name: di
parameters.description: Step between successive values; may be negative or non-integer.

tools.example:
Range[5]
Range[2, 10, 2]
Range[0, 1, 1/4]
Range[10, 1, -3]
tools.notes: With non-exact steps the endpoint may be excluded due to floating point; use Subdivide[a, b, n] when you need exactly n+1 points including both ends.

tools.name: Table
tools.description: Builds a list by evaluating an expression repeatedly over one or more iterators, in the same {i, imin, imax, di} form used by Sum and Do. Multiple iterators produce nested lists with the leftmost iterator varying slowest, which makes Table the standard way to construct matrices and tensors. Table has attribute HoldAll, so the body is not evaluated until the iterator variables have values.
tools.usage:
Table[expr, n]
Table[expr, {i, imax}]
Table[expr, {i, imin, imax, di}]
Table[expr, {i, {e1, e2, ...}}]
Table[expr, {i, ...}, {j, ...}]

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: Expression evaluated once per iteration; held until the iterators are assigned.

parameters.name: {i, imin, imax, di}
parameters.description: Iterator specification; a bare list {i, {a,b,c}} iterates over explicit values.

tools.example:
Table[i^2, {i, 1, 5}]
Table[i*j, {i, 3}, {j, 3}]
Table[x, {5}]
Table[f[s], {s, {a, b, c}}]
tools.notes: For large numeric arrays Array, ConstantArray or a Listable operation on Range is usually faster because Table evaluates its body symbolically each time. Use ParallelTable to spread iterations over parallel kernels.

tools.name: Array
tools.description: Creates an array by applying a function to index values. Array[f, n] gives {f[1], ..., f[n]}, and Array[f, {m, n}] gives a matrix whose (i,j) element is f[i, j]. An optional origin argument shifts the starting index, and an optional head replaces List in the result, which is handy for building symbolic structures.
tools.usage:
Array[f, n]
Array[f, {n1, n2, ...}]
Array[f, dims, origin]
Array[f, dims, origin, h]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function applied to the index or indices.

parameters.name: dims
parameters.description: Length, or list of lengths for a multidimensional array.

parameters.name: origin
parameters.description: Starting index value (default 1); may be a list for several dimensions.

parameters.name: h
parameters.description: Head to use in place of List, e.g. Plus or And.

tools.example:
Array[f, 4]
Array[#1 + #2 &, {2, 3}]
Array[a, 3, 0]
Array[x, 3, 1, Plus]
tools.notes: Unlike Table, Array evaluates f normally (it has no Hold attributes), so pure functions and Listable built-ins work directly.

tools.name: ConstantArray
tools.description: Creates an array of any shape whose elements are all the same expression. ConstantArray[c, n] gives a length-n list and ConstantArray[c, {m, n}] a m x n matrix. It is the fastest way to allocate a zero or constant matrix and produces a packed array when the constant is a machine number.
tools.usage:
ConstantArray[c, n]
ConstantArray[c, {n1, n2, ...}]
tools.example:
ConstantArray[0, 5]
ConstantArray[1.0, {3, 3}]
ConstantArray[x, {2, 2}]
tools.notes: For a large all-zero matrix that will stay mostly empty, SparseArray[{}, {m, n}] uses far less memory.

tools.name: Length
tools.description: Gives the number of elements at the top level of any expression, i.e. the number of arguments of its head. For a list this is the number of elements; for a matrix it is the number of rows. Length[atom] is 0 for numbers, symbols and strings.
tools.usage: Length[expr]
tools.example:
Length[{a, b, c, d}]
Length[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Length[a + b + c]
Length["abcd"]
tools.notes: Length of a String is 0 because strings are atoms; use StringLength instead. Use Dimensions for the full shape of a rectangular array and Depth for nesting level.

tools.name: Dimensions
tools.description: Gives the dimensions of a full (rectangular) nested list as a list of integers. Dimensions[m] returns {rows, columns} for a matrix and {} for a scalar, stopping at the first level that is not rectangular. An optional second argument limits how many levels are examined.
tools.usage:
Dimensions[expr]
Dimensions[expr, n]
tools.example:
Dimensions[{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}}]
Dimensions[Array[a, {2, 3, 4}]]
Dimensions[{{1, 2}, {3}}]
tools.notes: Ragged data gives a shorter result than you might expect; use ArrayQ or MatrixQ to test rectangularity first, and ArrayDepth for the number of rectangular levels.

tools.name: Part
tools.description: Extracts parts of an expression, written with double brackets as expr[[i]]. Indices count from 1, negative indices count from the end, All selects a whole level, a span i;;j selects a range, and a list of indices selects several parts at once. Successive index arguments descend into nested lists, so m[[2, 3]] is the element in row 2, column 3.
tools.usage:
expr[[i]]
expr[[i, j, ...]]
expr[[{i1, i2, ...}]]
expr[[i ;; j]]
Part[expr, i]
tools.notes: Part is also assignable: m[[1, 2]] = 0 modifies the stored value in place, which is the efficient way to update large arrays. expr[[0]] gives the head.

tools.name: First
tools.description: Gives the first element of a list or the first argument of any expression. A second argument supplies a default that is returned instead of raising a message when the expression is empty, which makes First safe inside larger pipelines. Commonly used with Cases, Position or Select to take the single result expected.
tools.usage:
First[expr]
First[expr, default]
tools.example:
First[{a, b, c}]
First[{}, None]
First[Cases[{1, x, 2}, _Integer]]
tools.notes: Related: Last, Rest, Most, Take. FirstCase[list, patt] combines Cases and First in one pass and is faster on long lists.

tools.name: Last
tools.description: Gives the last element of a list or the last argument of an expression, with an optional default for the empty case. Equivalent to expr[[-1]] but clearer in intent and safer with the default argument. Often used to take the final state from NestList, FoldList or a recurrence table.
tools.usage:
Last[expr]
Last[expr, default]
tools.example:
Last[{a, b, c}]
Last[{}, Missing[]]
Last[NestList[2 # &, 1, 10]]

tools.name: Rest
tools.description: Gives an expression with its first element removed. Together with First it forms the classic head/tail decomposition used in recursive list processing. Rest[{}] issues a message and stays unevaluated, so guard recursion with an empty-list base case.
tools.usage: Rest[expr]
tools.notes: Rest is O(n) because it copies the list; prefer Fold, Map or Total over deep recursion on long lists.

tools.name: Most
tools.description: Gives an expression with its last element removed, the mirror image of Rest. Frequently combined with Last, or used with Differences-style pairwise computations where the final element has no successor.
tools.usage: Most[expr]

tools.name: Take
tools.description: Takes a contiguous or strided selection of elements. Take[list, n] gives the first n, Take[list, -n] the last n, and Take[list, {m, n, s}] the elements from m to n in steps of s. Extra sequence arguments apply to successive levels, so Take[m, 2, 3] takes a 2x3 submatrix.
tools.usage:
Take[list, n]
Take[list, -n]
Take[list, {m, n}]
Take[list, {m, n, s}]
Take[list, seq1, seq2, ...]
tools.example:
Take[Range[10], 3]
Take[Range[10], -3]
Take[Range[10], {3, 8, 2}]
Take[Array[a, {4, 4}], 2, 3]
tools.notes: Take errors if fewer elements exist than requested; TakeWhile, TakeLargest and TakeDrop cover the common conditional variants. UpTo[n] can be used as a lenient length specification.

tools.name: Drop
tools.description: Returns a list with selected elements removed, using the same index specifications as Take. Drop[list, n] removes the first n elements, Drop[list, -n] the last n, and Drop[list, {m, n}] a contiguous block. Drop[list, {k}] removes a single element k.
tools.usage:
Drop[list, n]
Drop[list, -n]
Drop[list, {m, n}]
Drop[list, {k}]
tools.example:
Drop[Range[10], 3]
Drop[Range[10], -2]
Drop[Range[10], {4, 6}]
Drop[{a, b, c}, {2}]
tools.notes: Delete[list, i] is a clearer alternative for removing one element by position, and DeleteCases removes by pattern.

tools.name: Append
tools.description: Returns a new expression with an element added at the end; the original is unchanged because Wolfram Language values are immutable. AppendTo[x, e] performs the same operation and reassigns the symbol. Appending in a loop is O(n^2) on lists, so prefer Table, Reap/Sow or a Sow-based accumulator for large collections.
tools.usage:
Append[expr, elem]
AppendTo[symbol, elem]
tools.notes: For repeated growth use Internal`Bag, Reap/Sow, or preallocate with ConstantArray and assign with Part. Association and Dataset have their own Append behaviour for key/value pairs.

tools.name: Prepend
tools.description: Returns a new expression with an element added at the front, with PrependTo as the in-place reassigning form. Building a list by repeatedly prepending and then reversing is a common functional idiom, though Reap/Sow is usually faster. Works on any expression, not just lists.
tools.usage:
Prepend[expr, elem]
PrependTo[symbol, elem]

tools.name: Join
tools.description: Concatenates two or more lists (or any expressions sharing the same head) into one. An optional level specification joins along a deeper dimension, so Join[m1, m2, 2] glues matrices side by side. Joining Associations merges them with later keys winning.
tools.usage:
Join[list1, list2, ...]
Join[list1, list2, n]
tools.notes: All arguments must have the same head. Use Catenate or Flatten[list, 1] to join a list of lists that is already collected, and ArrayFlatten to assemble block matrices.

tools.name: Flatten
tools.description: Removes nested list structure. Flatten[list] flattens completely, Flatten[list, n] flattens only the top n levels, and Flatten[list, n, h] flattens expressions with head h. A list-of-lists index specification transposes and merges dimensions in one step, e.g. Flatten[t, {{1, 3}, {2}}].
tools.usage:
Flatten[list]
Flatten[list, n]
Flatten[list, n, h]
Flatten[list, {{i, j, ...}, ...}]
tools.notes: Flatten[list, 1] is the usual way to concatenate a list of lists; Catenate is equivalent and often faster. ArrayReshape is the right tool when you want to change shape rather than remove structure.

tools.name: Partition
tools.description: Splits a list into sublists of a given length, optionally with an offset that produces overlapping or sparse blocks. Partition[list, n] gives non-overlapping blocks discarding any remainder, while Partition[list, n, d] advances by d each time, so d = 1 gives all sliding windows. Padding arguments control how incomplete final blocks are handled, including cyclic padding.
tools.usage:
Partition[list, n]
Partition[list, n, d]
Partition[list, n, d, {kL, kR}, padding]
Partition[list, {n1, n2, ...}]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Block length (or list of lengths for multidimensional blocking).

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Offset between the start of successive blocks.

parameters.name: padding
parameters.description: Elements used to pad an incomplete block; {} means no padding and the remainder is kept short.

tools.example:
Partition[Range[9], 3]
Partition[Range[6], 2, 1]
Partition[Range[7], 3, 3, 1, {}]
Partition[Range[8], {2, 2}] (* only for matrices *)
tools.notes: Partition[list, 2, 1] is the standard idiom for consecutive pairs (e.g. computing differences or building edges). For a matrix, Partition[m, {r, c}] produces a block decomposition.

tools.name: Transpose
tools.description: Interchanges the first two levels of a nested list, turning rows into columns. Transpose[t, {n1, n2, ...}] permutes arbitrary tensor levels, and Transpose[m, {1, 1}] extracts the diagonal. Transposing a pair of equal-length lists is the standard way to zip them into coordinate pairs.
tools.usage:
Transpose[m]
Transpose[t, perm]
tools.notes: For complex matrices use ConjugateTranspose for the Hermitian adjoint. Thread[{xs, ys}] gives the same zip result as Transpose[{xs, ys}].

tools.name: Reverse
tools.description: Reverses the order of elements in a list or other expression. A level specification reverses at a deeper level, so Reverse[m, 2] reverses each row of a matrix and Reverse[m, {1, 2}] reverses both. Works on strings only via StringReverse.
tools.usage:
Reverse[expr]
Reverse[expr, n]
Reverse[expr, {n1, n2, ...}]

tools.name: RotateLeft
tools.description: Cyclically shifts elements toward the front, with elements falling off the start reappearing at the end. RotateLeft[list, n] rotates by n positions, and a list of offsets rotates successive levels of a tensor. RotateRight is the mirror operation; both are central to circular-buffer and cellular-automaton style code.
tools.usage:
RotateLeft[expr]
RotateLeft[expr, n]
RotateLeft[expr, {n1, n2, ...}]
tools.example:
RotateLeft[{a, b, c, d}]
RotateLeft[Range[6], 2]
RotateRight[Range[6], 2]
RotateLeft[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, {1, 1}]
tools.notes: Negative n rotates the other way, so RotateLeft[l, -1] equals RotateRight[l, 1].

tools.name: Sort
tools.description: Sorts a list into canonical order, or into the order defined by a supplied two-argument ordering predicate that returns True when its first argument should come first. Numbers sort numerically, strings lexicographically, and arbitrary expressions in the Wolfram Language canonical order. Sort is stable for equal elements when an explicit ordering function is given.
tools.usage:
Sort[list]
Sort[list, p]

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: Ordering function p[a, b] returning True if a should precede b, e.g. Greater or (#1[[2]] < #2[[2]] &).

tools.example:
Sort[{3, 1, 2}]
Sort[{3, 1, 2}, Greater]
Sort[{{2, "b"}, {1, "a"}}]
Sort[{"pear", "fig"}, StringLength[#1] < StringLength[#2] &]
tools.notes: SortBy is usually clearer and faster than Sort with a comparison function because it computes the key once per element (a Schwartzian transform).

tools.name: SortBy
tools.description: Sorts a list by the value of a function applied to each element, comparing the computed keys in canonical order. SortBy[list, {f1, f2}] sorts by f1 and breaks ties with f2. The operator form SortBy[f] is convenient inside pipelines and works on Associations and Datasets as well as lists.
tools.usage:
SortBy[list, f]
SortBy[list, {f1, f2, ...}]
SortBy[f][list]
tools.example:
SortBy[{{1, "c"}, {3, "a"}}, Last]
SortBy[Range[-5, 5], Abs]
SortBy[{<|"n" -> 2|>, <|"n" -> 1|>}, #n &]
SortBy[{"aaa", "b", "cc"}, StringLength]
tools.notes: Use Minus or a negated key to sort descending, e.g. SortBy[data, -#score &], or ReverseSortBy in recent versions.

tools.name: Ordering
tools.description: Gives the permutation of positions that would sort a list, so list[[Ordering[list]]] equals Sort[list]. Ordering[list, n] gives the positions of the n smallest elements and Ordering[list, -n] the n largest, which is the efficient way to find top-k items without a full sort. A third argument supplies a custom ordering function.
tools.usage:
Ordering[list]
Ordering[list, n]
Ordering[list, n, p]
tools.example:
Ordering[{30, 10, 20}]
Ordering[{30, 10, 20}, 2]
Ordering[{30, 10, 20}, -1]
scores = {5, 9, 1}; names = {"a", "b", "c"};
names[[Ordering[scores, -2]]]
tools.notes: Use Ordering to sort one list by the values of another. TakeLargest/TakeSmallest return the values themselves rather than positions.

tools.name: Union
tools.description: Gives a sorted list of the distinct elements of one or more lists, i.e. the set union with duplicates removed. Union[list] alone is the classic way to get sorted distinct values. A SameTest option lets you treat nearly equal reals or custom objects as identical.
tools.usage:
Union[list]
Union[list1, list2, ...]
Union[list1, list2, SameTest -> f]
tools.notes: Union sorts its result; use DeleteDuplicates when the original order must be preserved.

tools.name: Intersection
tools.description: Gives the sorted list of elements common to all the supplied lists, with duplicates removed. Together with Union and Complement it provides the standard set algebra on lists. A SameTest option customizes the equality test.
tools.usage:
Intersection[list1, list2, ...]
Intersection[list1, list2, SameTest -> f]
tools.example:
Intersection[{1, 2, 3, 4}, {3, 4, 5}]
Intersection[{a, b, c}, {b, c, d}, {c, d, e}]
tools.notes: For very large sets, converting to an Association or using Lookup/KeyExistsQ can be faster than repeated Intersection calls.

tools.name: Complement
tools.description: Gives the sorted list of elements that are in the first list but in none of the others, i.e. set difference. Duplicates are removed, so Complement always returns a set. Useful for finding missing keys, unmatched records or unused indices.
tools.usage: Complement[all, list1, list2, ...]
tools.example:
Complement[Range[10], {2, 4, 6}]
Complement[{a, b, c}, {b}]
Complement[{1, 1, 2}, {}]
tools.notes: Use DeleteCases or Select when the elements must stay in their original order or when matching by pattern rather than by exact value.

tools.name: DeleteDuplicates
tools.description: Removes repeated elements while keeping the first occurrence of each and preserving the original order. An optional two-argument test function defines what counts as a duplicate. DeleteDuplicatesBy removes duplicates according to a computed key, which is the usual choice for records.
tools.usage:
DeleteDuplicates[list]
DeleteDuplicates[list, test]
DeleteDuplicatesBy[list, f]
tools.example:
DeleteDuplicates[{3, 1, 3, 2, 1}]
DeleteDuplicatesBy[{{1, "a"}, {1, "b"}, {2, "c"}}, First]
DeleteDuplicates[{1.0, 1.001, 2.0}, Abs[#1 - #2] < 0.01 &]
tools.notes: Without a test function DeleteDuplicates is near-linear using hashing; supplying a test makes it quadratic, so prefer DeleteDuplicatesBy when possible.

tools.name: Position
tools.description: Gives a list of the positions at which a pattern occurs in an expression, each position expressed as an index list usable with Extract or ReplacePart. A level specification restricts the search depth, and Heads -> False excludes heads from consideration. Position searches all levels by default, so it finds matches inside nested structures.
tools.usage:
Position[expr, pattern]
Position[expr, pattern, levelspec]
Position[expr, pattern, levelspec, n]
tools.example:
Position[{a, b, a, c}, a]
Position[{{1, 2}, {3, 1}}, 1]
Position[{1, 2.5, 3}, _Real]
Position[{5, 3, 5}, 5, 1, 1]
tools.notes: Use FirstPosition for just the first match. Position returns {} when nothing matches, and Flatten[Position[list, x]] gives simple indices for a flat list.

tools.name: Select
tools.description: Picks out the elements of a list for which a predicate function returns True. Select[list, crit, n] stops after n matches, which avoids scanning the rest of a long list. The operator form Select[crit] composes cleanly in pipelines and also works on Associations, where keys are preserved.
tools.usage:
Select[list, crit]
Select[list, crit, n]
Select[crit][list]

parameters.name: crit
parameters.description: Predicate applied to each element; only elements giving True are kept (non-True results such as unevaluated conditions are dropped).

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Maximum number of elements to return.

tools.example:
Select[Range[20], PrimeQ]
Select[{1, -2, 3, -4}, Positive]
Select[Range[100], Divisible[#, 7] &, 3]
Select[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 5|>, # > 2 &]
tools.notes: Cases with a pattern is usually faster than Select with a predicate when the test is structural. Select requires literal True, so a predicate returning an unevaluated inequality silently filters everything out.

tools.name: Cases
tools.description: Gives the elements of an expression that match a pattern, optionally transformed by a replacement rule at the same time. A level specification searches deeper than level 1, making Cases the standard tool for harvesting subexpressions of a given form from anywhere in a structure. The count argument limits how many matches are returned.
tools.usage:
Cases[expr, pattern]
Cases[expr, pattern -> rhs]
Cases[expr, pattern, levelspec]
Cases[expr, pattern, levelspec, n]
tools.example:
Cases[{1, x, 2, y}, _Integer]
Cases[{f[1], g[2], f[3]}, f[n_] :> n]
Cases[Sin[x] + Cos[y]^2, _Symbol, Infinity]
Cases[Range[50], _?PrimeQ, 1, 5]
tools.notes: Cases[expr, patt, Infinity] is the idiomatic deep search. Use DeleteCases for the complement, Count to just count matches, and FirstCase for the first hit.

tools.name: Count
tools.description: Counts how many elements of an expression match a pattern, with an optional level specification for deeper searches. It is the direct way to tally occurrences without building an intermediate list. The operator form Count[pattern] works inside Map and Query.
tools.usage:
Count[expr, pattern]
Count[expr, pattern, levelspec]
Count[pattern][expr]
tools.notes: For counting all distinct values at once use Tally or Counts, which do a single pass.

tools.name: MemberQ
tools.description: Tests whether an expression contains an element matching a pattern at level 1, returning True or False. A level specification extends the test to deeper levels. Because it takes a pattern rather than a literal, MemberQ[list, _Integer] tests for any integer member.
tools.usage:
MemberQ[expr, form]
MemberQ[expr, form, levelspec]
MemberQ[form][expr]
tools.example:
MemberQ[{a, b, c}, b]
MemberQ[{1, 2.5}, _Real]
MemberQ[{{1, 2}, {3}}, 3, 2]
Select[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, MemberQ[#, 3] &]
tools.notes: For repeated membership tests on a large fixed set, build an Association and use KeyExistsQ or Lookup, which is O(1) instead of O(n).

tools.name: FreeQ
tools.description: Returns True if an expression contains nothing matching the given pattern anywhere (at any level, including heads by default). It is the logical complement of a deep MemberQ and is the standard guard in pattern conditions such as x_ /; FreeQ[x, y]. A level specification restricts where the search happens.
tools.usage:
FreeQ[expr, form]
FreeQ[expr, form, levelspec]
FreeQ[form][expr]
tools.example:
FreeQ[a + b, c]
FreeQ[Sin[x], x]
FreeQ[{1, 2, 3}, _Real]
Cases[{x + 1, y + 1}, e_ /; FreeQ[e, y]]
tools.notes: FreeQ looks at all levels including heads, so FreeQ[f[x], f] is False. Use MatchQ or Position when you need to know where a match occurred.

tools.name: Extract
tools.description: Extracts the parts of an expression at the positions given as index lists, exactly in the format produced by Position. Unlike Part it takes positions as data rather than as syntax, so it composes naturally with search results. An optional function argument is applied to each extracted part before it is returned, and it can be given Hold attributes to inspect parts without evaluating them.
tools.usage:
Extract[expr, pos]
Extract[expr, {pos1, pos2, ...}]
Extract[expr, pos, h]
tools.notes: Extract[expr, pos, Hold] is the standard trick for grabbing a subexpression without evaluating it.

tools.name: ReplacePart
tools.description: Returns a copy of an expression with parts at given positions replaced by new values. Positions use the same index-list form as Position and Extract, and a list of pos -> value rules replaces several parts at once. Unlike an assignment to Part it never modifies the original, which makes it safe inside functional code.
tools.usage:
ReplacePart[expr, i -> new]
ReplacePart[expr, {i1 -> n1, i2 -> n2}]
ReplacePart[expr, {i, j} -> new]
ReplacePart[new][expr]
tools.example:
ReplacePart[{a, b, c}, 2 -> x]
ReplacePart[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, {2, 1} -> 0]
ReplacePart[Range[5], {1 -> a, 5 -> z}]
tools.notes: For in-place modification of a large array, m[[i, j]] = v is much faster because it avoids copying.

tools.name: Insert
tools.description: Inserts an element at a specified position, shifting later elements along. Negative positions count from the end, so Insert[list, x, -1] appends. A list of positions inserts the same element at several places at once.
tools.usage:
Insert[expr, elem, n]
Insert[expr, elem, {i, j, ...}]
Insert[expr, elem, {{p1}, {p2}}]

tools.name: Delete
tools.description: Removes the element or elements at the given positions, using the index-list format shared with Position and Extract. Delete[expr, {{p1}, {p2}}] removes several parts in one pass. It is the position-based counterpart of DeleteCases, which removes by pattern.
tools.usage:
Delete[expr, i]
Delete[expr, {i, j}]
Delete[expr, {{i1}, {i2}, ...}]
tools.example:
Delete[{a, b, c, d}, 2]
Delete[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, {1, 2}]
Delete[Range[6], {{2}, {4}}]
Delete[list, Position[list, 0]]
tools.notes: Positions are interpreted against the original expression, so deleting several positions at once is safe and does not require adjusting indices.

tools.name: Riffle
tools.description: Interleaves elements between the elements of a list, most often to insert separators. Riffle[list, x] places x between every pair, while Riffle[list, {a, b, ...}] cycles through the given elements. A {m, n, s} specification controls exactly which gaps are filled.
tools.usage:
Riffle[list, x]
Riffle[list, {x1, x2, ...}]
Riffle[list, x, {m, n, s}]
tools.example:
Riffle[{a, b, c}, x]
Riffle[{1, 2, 3}, {"+", "-"}]
StringJoin[Riffle[{"a", "b", "c"}, ", "]]
tools.notes: For strings, StringRiffle is more direct and handles nesting and separators for rows and columns.
